newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs to kickstart infrastructure - analysts.
newsitem.headline: India needs to kickstart infrastructure - analysts.

text.p: The Indian government must put up some money if it wants to get the ball rolling in its ambitious quest for foreign investment in infrastructure, analysts said on Wednesday.

They said the reluctance of skittish investors to fund infrastructure projects and the inexperience of government officials in dealing with such projects had replaced corruption and red tape as the main hurdles in wooing investment in power plants, roads and ports.
"The downside is huge (for private investors)," said Shaun Browne, director, equity capital markets at HSBC Investment Bank Plc.
"The only way for the government is to come into partnership with some funding, certainly in the early projects," he said.

Frequent power cuts, long waiting lists for telephones, narrow highways and clogged ports unable to cope with growing demand for imports have stymied official plans for high economic growth since India launched a free-market programme in 1991.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, chairing a brainstorming session with industrialists on infrastructure on Tuesday, cited corruption as a key factor blocking the investment drive.

Several decisions were taken at the meeting, such as allowing power companies to use the fuel storage facilities of state-run oil companies if needed, and expanding the equity base of state power companies to make their financial bases stronger and help them increase their borrowings to fund new projects.
Officials also said they would take steps to strengthen legal assurances for prospective investors.
"The government has been quite positive in sending out the right signals to foreign investors," Nitin Anandkar, power industry analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking, said in Bombay.
The government estimates India needs $150 billion worth of infrastructure investments over five years.
But infrastructure companies have faced numerous problems such as delays in obtaining environmental safety clearances and high prices for electricity.
More recently, investments have been stalled by administrative delays caused by officials who have no precedents to fall back on in India's still-young reform drive.
There is also a reluctance among bankers to plunge into a virgin investment area.
"I doubt if corruption and red tape are the problems," one investment analyst said. "A lot of it is nervousness and inexperience."
Anandkar said it would be unrealistic to hope that corruption could be swept away overnight.

A scarcity of adequate roads, power, telecommunication facilities and ports are being cited among key reasons for a slowdown in India's industrial growth, which in 1996/97 (April-March) slumped to 6.7 percent from 11.6 percent the previous year.

India's economy grew by 6.8 percent in 1996/97. The government says it is aiming for a sustained annual seven percent growth in gross domestic product every year, and infrastructure is crucial to attaining this end.
